The ‘Cornell 7’ Fallout Is Infantilized Women And Villainized Men

Jane Doe, a former Cornell University student, alleges she was gang-raped by seven men at a Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. She claims she was intoxicated and under the influence of ketamine during the incident. Her lawsuit names the Chi Phi fraternity, the Tri Delta sorority, and Cornell University as defendants. The case has sparked widespread protests and debates over campus sexual misconduct and Title IX policies. Jane Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, has argued that the responsibility for ensuring her safety rested with others, and that she concealed her intoxication from authority figures. In text messages obtained by CBS News, Jane Doe and two fraternity members discussed the incident, with one expressing regret over the events. Cornell University has since banned all fraternity parties and announced new policies to improve support for survivors of sexual assault.

Where the accounts differ

The Federalist reports that Jane Doe’s lawsuit does not claim she was forced, only that she wasn’t capable of taking responsibility for her actions because she got drunk. The Federalist attributes this to Jane Doe’s own contemporaneous account. Slate states that Jane Doe’s complaint describes a 360-degree failure on the part of Cornell and the Greek life it supports, including that she left her sorority house to bar hop before stumbling to the Chi Phi fraternity. The Nation claims that Jane Doe’s complaint to the Cornell University Police Department was minimized by the police, omitting the fact that she claimed to have been raped. CBS News reports that Jane Doe’s lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, described her messages as “classic symptoms of delayed recognition” and called it “a textbook response to sexual assault.” The Nation also states that the district attorney declined to bring charges after an investigation in 2024. The BBC reports that Cornell’s president said the school would allow New York State Police’s trauma-informed officers to investigate allegations of sexual assault on its campus. The Federalist and Slate differ on the nature of the incident, with the Federalist referring to it as a “gangbang” and Slate as a “gang rape.” The Nation and CBS News differ on the legal outcome, with the Nation stating that the district attorney declined to bring charges and CBS News stating that the district attorney declined to bring charges after an investigation in 2024.

Sources The Federalist · Slate · The Nation · CBS News · BBC · FOX News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump's Russia diesel deal and Ukraine's Starlink restrictions spark controversy

President Donald Trump announced a deal to import 3 million tons of Russian diesel over the coming months, aiming to lower U.S. fuel prices. The deal, which includes a temporary waiver of sanctions on Russian oil exports, has drawn criticism from lawmakers and analysts. Diesel prices in the U.S. have remained high, averaging $6.27 per gallon, with analysts noting that the deal would only provide a small fraction of the country's daily diesel consumption. Meanwhile, Ukraine reported restrictions on its use of Starlink and Starshield satellite services, which are critical for military operations. Ukrainian officials suspect the restrictions were intentional, possibly linked to Trump's public criticism of President Zelensky.

The U.S. Treasury Department temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel exports, allowing the country to sell the fuel globally. However, the deal has faced pushback from both Democrats and some Republicans, who argue it undermines sanctions and could benefit Russia's war efforts. Analysts suggest that the global diesel shortage, driven by conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, is a more significant factor in high prices than the Trump-Russia deal.

Where the accounts differ

NPR states that Trump claimed Russia would release 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and global markets immediately, while Straight Arrow News reports that the deal includes 3 million tons of diesel over the coming months. Axios and The Hill describe the Starlink restrictions as a potential act of retaliation against Ukraine for attacking Russian refineries, while Washington Examiner links the restrictions to Trump's public criticism of Zelensky. The Hill and Axios attribute the Starlink restrictions to SpaceX, while The Hill also notes that Musk pointed the finger at the U.S. government for imposing limits on Starshield.

Sources NPR · Axios · The Hill · Straight Arrow News · Christian Science Monitor · Washington Examiner

Houthis Launch Attacks on Saudi Airports, Sparking Escalation in Regional Conflict

The Houthis, an Iran-backed group, launched attacks on Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, killing at least 12 people, including an American citizen, and injuring over 300. The attacks disrupted air travel and raised concerns about Saudi Arabia’s ability to defend its territory. In response, Saudi Arabia launched strikes on a Yemeni oil depot and intercepted missiles aimed at its energy infrastructure, including the headquarters of Saudi Aramco. President Donald Trump warned the Houthis against further attacks and suggested the U.S. might consider military action. The conflict, which dates back to 2014, has seen escalating violence, with both sides targeting each other’s energy and military assets.

The Houthis have intensified their attacks, including strikes on Saudi airports and oil facilities, which they claim are in retaliation for Saudi air strikes in Yemen. Saudi Arabia has accused the Houthis of seeking to disrupt global energy supplies and has vowed to hold them accountable. The conflict has also drawn international attention, with the International Monetary Fund warning of potential negative economic spillovers. Meanwhile, Trump has criticized the Houthis for their actions and hinted at possible U.S. involvement, though he has not announced any specific military measures.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire reports that at least 20 people were killed and 356 injured in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports between October 6 and October 11, while The Guardian and BBC report that the deadliest attack on October 10 killed 13 people. The Guardian and BBC also mention that the Saudi-led coalition intercepted missiles aimed at Dharan, the location of Saudi Aramco’s headquarters, while The Daily Wire does not mention this interception. The Guardian and BBC attribute the warning about the oil depot to Saudi authorities, while The Daily Wire attributes a warning to Houthi official Mohammed al-Bukhaiti. The New York Post and CBS News do not mention the specific casualty numbers from the airport attacks, focusing instead on Trump’s response and the broader regional context.

Sources The Daily Wire · The Guardian · BBC · Christian Science Monitor · New York Post · CBS News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Major U.S. Bank Hit With $1.21 Billion In Penalties After Ignoring Red Flags

The Treasury Department announced more than $1.21 billion in penalties against Bank of America for anti-money laundering and sanctions violations. The enforcement actions include the largest fine in the history of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the third-largest penalty in Treasury history. According to Treasury, Bank of America failed to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions on time, including activity indicative of Chinese money laundering networks. The bank also processed hundreds of payments that appeared to violate U.S. sanctions targeting Iran, Russia, and other countries. Bank of America admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain an adequate anti-money laundering program, conduct required checks on accounts for foreign financial institutions, and file suspicious activity reports. The bank said it will record a $1.2 billion, non-tax-deductible charge in its third-quarter results, reducing net income by about 17 cents per share.

Treasury investigators found that the bank relied heavily on law enforcement inquiries and warnings from other financial institutions to identify suspicious activity instead of using its own systems to flag potential problems. The bank also allowed suspicious transactions to go uninvestigated for extended periods, delaying reports to authorities. Treasury said it failed to respond promptly to concerns about customers receiving payments from unknown third parties, including potential connections to narcotics trafficking proceeds. Key compliance staff lacked adequate training, and internal audits failed to identify longstanding problems later uncovered by regulators.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and Fox Business both mention the $1.21 billion total penalty, including the $750 million from the OCC and the $11.6 million from OFAC. The New York Post and Newsweek also report the $1.2 billion penalty, but Newsweek notes that the $750 million from the OCC is credited against the $1.2 billion penalty, not added to it. The BBC and Axios both state that the $1.2 billion penalty includes the $750 million from the OCC and the $11.6 million from OFAC. The Daily Wire and Fox Business mention the $1.21 billion total, while the New York Post and Newsweek refer to the $1.2 billion penalty. The Daily Wire and Fox Business also note that the $1.2 billion penalty includes the $750 million from the OCC and the $11.6 million from OFAC, while the New York Post and Newsweek do not specify the breakdown of the penalty.

Sources The Daily Wire · Axios · Newsweek · BBC · Fox Business · New York Post

No source labeled left covered this story.

Judge blocks Trump's White House ban targeting CNN, MS NOW and Politico

A federal judge ruled that President Trump cannot ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from covering him at the White House, at least temporarily. The judge found that Trump's decision to revoke the press credentials of more than 70 journalists from these outlets likely violated their First Amendment and due process rights. The news organizations filed a lawsuit after the Trump administration denied them access, and the judge granted a temporary restraining order on Sept. 24. The ruling was issued after the Justice Department announced it would appeal the decision. The White House criticized the ruling, calling the outlets "Fake News" and claiming they are capable of reporting from outside the White House.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and CBS News both state that the judge ruled Trump's ban violated the First Amendment and due process rights, but NPR mentions that the judge specifically cited Trump's public statements and social media posts to support his conclusion. CBS News adds that the judge rejected the administration's claims about national security concerns. Axios and Newsweek both note that the judge ordered the White House to reinstate press access, but Axios highlights that the judge's ruling does not guarantee access to key areas like the Oval Office. Straight Arrow News and The Guardian both mention that the judge found the ban likely violated the First Amendment, but Straight Arrow News adds that the judge questioned the administration's national security justification, noting that Trump raised those concerns only after the credentials were revoked.

Sources NPR · CBS News · Axios · Newsweek · Straight Arrow News · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Consumer inflation rose faster than expected in September, CPI report shows

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported that the consumer price index (CPI) increased 0.6% on a monthly basis in September, with an annual rate of 3.7%. Energy prices rose 5.2% monthly, contributing significantly to the inflation spike. Gasoline prices increased 9.1% from the prior month and are up 34.2% from a year ago. Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and food prices, rose 0.3% monthly and 2.6% annually. The report highlights persistent inflation pressures, with energy costs and other factors driving price increases.

The report comes ahead of the November midterm elections, with rising consumer prices becoming a major issue for both political parties. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 to combat inflation, lifting the target range to 3.75%-4.0%. Analysts suggest the Fed may need to continue raising rates as inflation remains above its 2% target.

Where the accounts differ

Fox Business and The Guardian both report that gasoline prices increased 9.1% from the prior month in September, while The Daily Wire and CBS News report the same figure. The Guardian and CBS News attribute the rise in energy prices to the U.S. war with Iran, while The Daily Wire also mentions the conflict with Iran as a cause. The Guardian and CBS News note that fuel oil prices increased 74% from last year, a detail not included in Fox Business or The Daily Wire. The Daily Wire and The Guardian mention Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's comments about inflation returning to the Fed's target after the Iran conflict ends, which is not included in Fox Business or CBS News. The Guardian and CBS News report that the September inflation rate is the highest before a midterm election since 1990, a claim not made by Fox Business or The Daily Wire.

Sources Fox Business · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · NPR · Axios · CBS News

OpenAI worker charged after recording device found in company conference room

A Saudi national, Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested and charged with attempting to secretly record confidential conversations at OpenAI’s San Francisco offices. The Department of Justice announced the arrest on Tuesday, stating that the device was discovered in an executive conference room. Alfozan, who had worked at OpenAI since July 2025, was arrested on October 9 after security personnel found the concealed recording device. OpenAI stated it has terminated his employment and referred the matter to the FBI. The FBI investigation is ongoing, with no indication that Alfozan improperly accessed or exfiltrated sensitive data.

Alfozan was allegedly using a productivity AI assistant to inquire about meeting rooms and schedules at OpenAI. The complaint also mentions that a chatbot account associated with his spouse submitted prompts related to building and installing a recording device. Security footage showed Alfozan near the conference room multiple times in September, despite lacking authorization to access it. On October 5, he was filmed entering the room and appearing to look behind the television where the device had been inserted. A second recording device was found in an unattended bag left by Alfozan in another room.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and CBS News both state that Alfozan was arrested on October 9, while the Al Jazeera article mentions that prosecutors disclosed the alleged flight booking to a judge on October 8. The BBC and Fox Business report that Alfozan was scheduled to fly to Saudi Arabia on October 12, a detail not mentioned in the Washington Examiner or CBS News accounts. The Daily Caller and Fox Business both mention that Alfozan wrapped the device in toilet paper, while the BBC and CBS News describe the device as being concealed in toilet paper. The Al Jazeera article notes that Alfozan’s lawyer, William Pernik, commented on the case, a detail not included in the Washington Examiner or CBS News accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · Al Jazeera · BBC · CBS News · Fox Business · The Daily Caller

No source labeled left covered this story.

Talarico’s Absence From Campaign Trail Sparks Speculation About Health

Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico was absent from the campaign trail for over a week, prompting speculation about his health. His campaign claimed he was recovering from a severe case of the flu, and he later appeared at an event where he described himself as feeling better. However, his absence raised questions, especially after conservative figures and media outlets suggested he might have been receiving mental health treatment. Talarico denied these claims, stating he had never been to Ohio, where some alleged he received care. The New York Times later reported that surveillance footage showed Talarico at his Austin home during his absence, supporting his account of being ill.

Talarico faced scrutiny during a CNN town hall where voters questioned his positions on issues like abortion, Israel’s actions in Gaza, and his views on God. He defended his past comments about God being nonbinary, citing religious figures like Pope Benedict and Charlie Kirk. Talarico also addressed the mental health rumors, calling them part of a “rage economy” fueled by online conspiracies. His Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, has faced his own controversies, including impeachment and a divorce filing by his wife.

Where the accounts differ

The Federalist reports that Talarico claimed to have visited his primary care physician in Austin and an urgent care facility in Dallas, but the timeline conflicts with flight data. The Guardian and FOX News both mention the false mental health rumors, with FOX News noting that Talarico’s campaign provided surveillance footage to the New York Times to debunk the claims. The Guardian states that Talarico denied ever being in Ohio, while The Federalist and FOX News both attribute the denial to Talarico himself. The Washington Examiner and The Dispatch do not mention the health speculation or the town hall event, focusing instead on Talarico’s debate format and a Paxton scandal, respectively.

Sources The Federalist · The Guardian · Washington Examiner · The Dispatch · FOX News · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Massive breach of Republican voter and donor data threatens election integrity and personal privacy for thousands.

Former Special Counsel Jack Smith obtained personal data on 639,000 Republican voters and donors, including MAGA hat buyers

Former Special Counsel Jack Smith and the Biden Justice Department collected personal information on over 639,000 Republican voters, donors, and supporters, including details such as names, addresses, and credit card information, according to a memo released by Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley. The data included information on individuals who purchased red MAGA hats and Trump memorabilia, including shipping addresses. Grassley criticized the collection of such data as "invasive" and beyond what was necessary for the investigation. Smith’s team also obtained information on Trump campaign products such as hats, t-shirts, mugs, and door mats.

The memo, obtained by multiple outlets, revealed that Smith’s office collected data on donors who contributed as little as $1, and that the information spanned from 2005 to 2021. Grassley stated that the data collection was part of an effort to "map out the entire Republican Party apparatus." Smith, during a Senate hearing, confirmed that his team acquired financial information but could not recall every subpoena issued.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that Grassley’s memo includes a claim that Smith’s team obtained "spreadsheets containing Republican campaign donors, supporters, and detailed personal voter information in various formats, totaling over 639,000 individuals, at minimum," and that "over 148,000 rows are identified in the spreadsheets as donors." The New York Post and The Federalist both cite this same figure, but The Daily Caller reports a slightly higher number of 640,000. The Federalist also notes that the data included "last four digits of credit card numbers" and "donor analysis data (such as one-time versus recurring donations and the amount of the donation)," which are not mentioned in the other accounts. FOX News and The Daily Caller both mention that Smith’s team obtained information on the sales of red MAGA hats and their buyers, while The New York Post and The Federalist also include this detail. The Daily Caller adds that Smith’s team obtained "banking information" on thousands of donors, including "home addresses, bank account and routing numbers and signatures," which is not mentioned in the other accounts.

Federal agents raided Rep. Ilhan Omar’s DC home as part of an immigration investigation

Federal law enforcement agents executed a search warrant at Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, D.C., home on Monday morning, according to the Department of Justice and reports from Fox News and the Associated Press. The Justice Department stated the search was part of an ongoing criminal investigation. Omar responded to the raid with a fundraising message, calling the action “the latest step in their ludicrous, partisan investigation into my immigration status” and framing it as an attempt by the Trump administration to “target political enemies and weaponize law enforcement.” The search reportedly focused on Omar’s immigration paperwork, which her late father filled out when she was a child, according to unnamed sources cited by Fox News. The New York Times reported that the Justice Department had previously investigated Omar’s finances and interactions with a foreign citizen during Biden’s presidency, though the investigation stalled without charges.

The search has reignited debates about the legitimacy of the investigation, with some outlets suggesting it is part of a broader effort to scrutinize Omar’s immigration history. The Daily Wire and The Federalist reported that the investigation centers on Omar’s father’s immigration records, which may have been incomplete or inaccurate. The New York Post highlighted that Omar’s father, Nur Omar Mohamed, has no official record of being a naturalized U.S. citizen, according to documents obtained by a Minnesota activist in 2023.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and The Guardian both describe Omar as soliciting donations after the raid, with the Examiner citing a fundraising text message and the Guardian noting her social media response. The Slate article, however, does not mention any fundraising activity and instead focuses on the broader context of Trump’s alleged political motivations. The Daily Wire and The Federalist provide more detailed accounts of Omar’s personal history, including her marriage to her alleged biological brother, which other outlets either omit or only briefly mention. The New York Post and The Guardian both reference the lack of official records for Omar’s father, while The Federalist adds context about his military service under a Somali dictator.

Sources Washington Examiner · Slate · New York Post · The Daily Wire · The Federalist · The Guardian

Death on Six Flags rollercoaster in US triggers ride closures across six states

A man died and several others were injured after an incident involving a rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday. The park temporarily closed nine similar rollercoasters across six of its amusement parks as a precaution. Authorities and Six Flags have not confirmed the cause of the death or the nature of the injuries. Witnesses reported seeing a man fall from the Goliath rollercoaster, hitting other passengers before landing on the roof of a haunted house attraction. The incident has prompted an investigation by Cobb County police.

The Goliath rollercoaster, which opened in 2006, reaches speeds of 70mph and heights of 200 feet. It is described as a "hyper coaster" with a construction cost of $20 million. The ride has a history of incidents, including a 2006 death of a 45-year-old man attributed to a congenital heart condition. The park has also recently closed its X2 rollercoaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California following lawsuits related to serious injuries.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and CBS News both report that the man who died was identified as Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem of Atlanta, while the other accounts do not mention his name. The Daily Wire and The Guardian mention that the man was on the ride with a child, a detail not included in the other accounts. FOX News and The Guardian attribute the claim about the man's son being seated beside him to an unnamed woman, while the other accounts do not mention this. The Washington Examiner does not specify the number of injured people, while The Guardian and CBS News state that several others were injured. The Daily Wire and The Guardian mention that witnesses saw the man fall and hit other passengers three times, while the other accounts do not specify the number of impacts.

Sources The Guardian · Newsweek · Washington Examiner · FOX News · The Daily Wire · CBS News

Trump ousts Kimberly Guilfoyle as US ambassador to Greece after corruption allegations

President Donald Trump's administration has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign from her position as US ambassador to Greece, according to White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia. Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host, was facing mounting scrutiny over reports she allegedly asked a Trump donor to pay her hefty credit card bill in exchange for access to the administration and behaved inappropriately while in Athens. Trump said on Tuesday that she had done a good job, but will "not be there" in Greece any longer. "I didn't like what I read," he said. Guilfoyle vowed to defend herself, calling the claims false, and said the ambassadorship had been the "honour of a lifetime". Zacharia announced during her first - and unusually short - media briefing that Guilfoyle "had been asked to resign" without providing more details. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," she said. Guilfoyle, the 57-year-old ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom, was first nominated as envoy to Athens in December 2024, a month before Trump returned to the White House as president. Around the same time, news broke that she had broken up with Donald Trump Jr, to whom she was engaged.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that Guilfoyle was asked to resign by the White House, while Axios states she announced her resignation shortly after being asked to step down. The New York Post and The Daily Wire describe the White House as asking her to resign, but do not mention her announcing resignation. The Washington Examiner does not mention the resignation or the allegations against Guilfoyle. The Hill focuses on the broader context of Trump's scandals and does not detail the specific allegations against Guilfoyle. The Daily Wire and BBC both mention that Guilfoyle allegedly asked Eric Deters to wire money to her American Express bill, while The New York Post and The Hill do not specify the nature of the financial request. The Wall Street Journal is cited by BBC and Axios as the source of the text messages, but The Daily Wire does not name a specific outlet for the messages. The New York Post and The Daily Wire mention that Guilfoyle's lawyers disputed the authenticity of the messages, while the BBC and Axios attribute the dispute to her lawyers.

Sources BBC · Washington Examiner · Axios · New York Post · The Daily Wire · The Hill

Pope Leo XIV diagnosed with lung cancer, undergoes successful surgery to remove lower lobe of right lung

Pope Leo XIV was diagnosed with lung cancer and underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, the Vatican announced Tuesday. The procedure, performed at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, was successful and lasted about 90 minutes. The Pope awoke normally after the surgery and returned to his room following a brief observation period. The Vatican confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, which was suspected by preoperative tests and confirmed during the procedure. The Pope, who is 71 years old, has not been known to smoke and has a family history of cancer, including his mother and older brother.

The Vatican stated that the Pope's schedule has been cleared for the next several days, with no planned changes to his hospitalization, which is set at one week. The Pope announced the operation during his weekly Angelus blessing on Sunday, stating the nodule was detected at an early stage and was well localized. The Vatican has not yet announced further treatment plans.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that the Pope's surgery involved removing the lower lobe of his right lung and that the Vatican has not announced further treatments. Axios states that the Pope was in the operating room for approximately three hours, while the surgery itself lasted 90 minutes. BBC mentions that the entire lower lobe was removed to ensure a radical procedure and includes quotes from Cardinal Kikuchi Tarcisio Isao and Carla and Elsa, who were present at the hospital. The Hill notes that the Vatican has not announced a change to the Pope's planned trip to South America. Straight Arrow News adds that the surgery used a video-assisted technique and includes a promotional message for their app. Just The News states that the surgery was led by Dr. Stefano Margaritora and that the Pope was in the operating room for three hours.

Sources NPR · Axios · BBC · The Hill · Straight Arrow News · Just The News

No source labeled left covered this story.

US midterm elections: 10 under-the-radar races worth watching

The Guardian highlights 10 under-the-radar races in the upcoming US midterm elections, noting that while marquee races receive more attention, lower-profile contests could result in upsets. Democrats are favored in most races, but Republicans are investing heavily in these contests. The article details specific races, including New Hampshire, Kansas, and Minnesota, where Democrats face challenges from Republican candidates. In New Hampshire, the race is considered a tossup due to the state's split-ticket voting habits. In Kansas, a medical billing scandal has impacted the Republican incumbent. In Minnesota, the race is close due to the progressive stance of the Democratic nominee and past fraud scandals.

The article also mentions Florida’s 13th congressional district and Wisconsin’s first congressional district, where Democrats are attempting to unseat Republican incumbents. The Guardian emphasizes the potential for a blue wave, with Democrats having a strong edge in most races, though some races are considered competitive.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Axios both mention the Kansas Senate race, but Axios adds that Democrat Adam Hamilton is the pastor of the largest United Methodist church in the country, while The Guardian notes that Republican Roger Marshall faced a medical billing scandal. FOX News and The Guardian both mention the Ohio Senate race, but FOX News attributes the medical billing scandal to Roger Marshall, while The Guardian attributes it to the Republican incumbent in Kansas. The Daily Wire and Just The News both mention Hillary Clinton’s new podcast, but The Daily Wire attributes the idea to Kara Swisher, while Just The News states that the idea came after a meeting in Washington’s Kalorama neighborhood.

Sources The Guardian · Axios · FOX News · The Daily Wire · Just The News · Newsweek

Trump insists Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire is real ‘because I said they agree’

President Donald Trump claimed on Sunday that a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on energy matters is in effect, asserting that both sides agreed to the deal. In a Truth Social post, Trump warned against breaking the agreement. Meanwhile, Ukrainian officials told The Daily Caller that they were not informed of the ceasefire and that no official agreement was reached. The Daily Caller reported that Ukrainian representatives confirmed they were not part of the negotiations before Trump made the announcement.

The Russian diesel deal, which Trump announced in an Oct. 9 Truth Social post, has drawn criticism from some Republicans, including Rep. Don Bacon and Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, who called for blocking Russian oil purchases. The deal, which Trump claimed would lower diesel prices, has also been questioned by Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who said there is no reason to believe the deal is authentic and that the administration has not followed the required congressional consultation process.

The White House has defended the decision, with a spokesperson stating that Trump is focused on bringing down costs for American consumers. However, energy analysts have expressed skepticism about the deal’s impact on diesel prices, which have remained high despite the announcement.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner claims that Trump stated Russia did not agree to the ceasefire protecting Ukraine’s energy facilities, while The Daily Caller reports that Ukrainian officials confirmed they were not informed of the ceasefire and that no agreement was reached. The Daily Caller also notes that Russia continued to attack Ukrainian energy infrastructure after Trump’s announcement, contradicting the Washington Examiner’s claim that the ceasefire is in effect. The Daily Caller and The Daily Caller both report that Ukrainian officials were not informed of the ceasefire, while the Washington Examiner does not mention this. The Daily Caller also states that Russia struck a power plant in Kyiv with a Shahed drone, causing power outages, which the Washington Examiner does not mention.

Sources Washington Examiner · FOX News · NPR · The Dispatch · Axios · The Daily Caller

No source labeled left covered this story.

Letitia James’ ‘fair’ Cornell rape probe vow collides with accused aide’s ‘quiet’ exit

New York Attorney General Letitia James has pledged a full and fair investigation into the Cornell 7 gang rape allegations, years after she faced accusations that she ignored warnings of sexual misconduct against her former chief of staff and allowed him to "quietly resign" while allegedly keeping his accuser in the dark. The claims stemmed from a 2022 lawsuit filed by James' former deputy press secretary, Sofia Quintanar. A New York judge dismissed the claims against James personally and the Attorney General's Office in February 2025. The decision was upheld by an appellate court in May 2026. Those allegations against James have received new attention after New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James as special prosecutor to investigate an alleged gang rape at a fraternity house associated with Cornell University in October 2024.

James is already facing calls to recuse herself from the case after an attorney for one of the defendants pointed to social media posts she made days before her appointment that appeared to take the alleged victim’s side. A spokesperson for James told Fox News Digital that James "has always taken these matters seriously and followed the facts and the law." Others, including fraud investigator Sam Antar, say New Yorkers shouldn't move on from the previous allegations raised against James by her former employee.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that a New York judge dismissed the claims against James personally and the Attorney General's Office in February 2025, with the decision upheld by an appellate court in May 2026. The Daily Wire and CBS News do not mention the court rulings against the claims against James personally, only that the civil lawsuit brought renewed attention to the case. The Daily Wire also reports that the district attorney declined to bring charges after an investigation in 2024, while CBS News states that the district attorney declined to bring charges after an investigation in 2024. The Daily Wire and CBS News both report that the accuser, Jane Doe, sent texts to the accused men, including one where she said "non of the sexual stuff was illegal" and "our body our choice asf." FOX News does not mention these texts, only that James made public comments about the case.

Sources FOX News · The Daily Wire · Mother Jones · Slate · The Nation · CBS News

Saudi Arabia further suspends flights after latest deadly Houthi attack on airport

Saudi Arabia has suspended all flights to and from its main international airport in Riyadh until next Saturday following a Houthi missile attack that killed one person and injured over 300. The attack occurred on Saturday, with additional strikes on Monday. The Houthis have also targeted oil facilities and other airports, including King Fahd International Airport in Dammam. Saudi authorities have canceled flights, with airlines such as Gulf Air and Etihad Airways suspending operations. The Saudi energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman, addressed the WPC Energy Conference, emphasizing the need for resilience and the importance of energy security. The Houthis have vowed to continue attacks on Saudi airports, warning that US involvement in Yemen would provoke a "swift and painful response."

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that the Houthi missile attack on Saturday killed 13 people and injured over 300, while Al Jazeera and BBC state the death toll was at least 13 with over 300 injured. The Guardian and BBC mention a Pakistani man was killed on Sunday, while Al Jazeera does not specify the number of casualties from Sunday’s attack. The Guardian and BBC note that the Saudi energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman, addressed the WPC Energy Conference, while Al Jazeera and The Christian Science Monitor also mention his remarks. The Daily Wire and New York Post focus on the political and religious implications of the attacks, while The Guardian and BBC provide more detailed accounts of the casualties and the closure of the airport. The Christian Science Monitor and BBC mention the closure of King Khalid International Airport until Saturday, while The Guardian and Al Jazeera state the closure is until next Saturday.

Sources The Guardian · Al Jazeera · BBC · The Daily Wire · Christian Science Monitor · New York Post

Hackers targeted refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets, raising temperatures to 122°F and causing fires and food spoilage

Hackers remotely accessed refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets, raising temperatures to as high as 122°F (50°C), which led to food spoilage and fires at several stores. The Paris prosecutor’s office described the attack as “large-scale,” affecting connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu ordered France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) to investigate, with officials coordinating with European counterparts due to potential cross-border impacts. The attack disrupted the cold chain, leading to the destruction of fresh and frozen products, with affected stores instructed to discard spoiled food.

The attack targeted refrigeration systems from Danish company Danfoss, which manage temperature settings for store freezers and fridges. Danfoss stated that affected units were running outdated firmware and had been advised to update or replace older systems. Cybersecurity firm Claroty had previously published research on vulnerabilities in Danfoss systems that could allow attackers to bypass authentication. French authorities and Danfoss have not yet linked these flaws to the recent attack. Some affected stores have resumed operations, though others continue to assess damage.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera reports that Intermarche said 300 of its Netto brand stores were targeted, while Straight Arrow News states Intermarché said between 150 and 200 stores were affected. The Daily Wire claims Les Mousquetaires said 180 of its stores were impacted. Al Jazeera and The Daily Wire mention that Intermarché CEO Thierry Cotillard estimated losses at “tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day,” while Straight Arrow News attributes the same quote to Cotillard but does not specify the timeframe. Al Jazeera and The Daily Wire note that Danfoss identified the affected units as “legacy” products no longer receiving updates, while Straight Arrow News states Danfoss said the affected units were running outdated firmware and had been advised to update.

Trump privately expresses doubts about livestreaming execution

President Trump has privately shared misgivings about livestreaming the firing-squad execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, according to four people who have spoken with the president. Trump has been receiving "negative input" about the idea from a bipartisan chorus of lawmakers and advisers, a senior administration official said. A livestream of Hasan's execution on Dec. 3 "might not happen," Trump told one confidant, who doesn't work in the administration and shared the comment with Axios. "He didn't sound particularly enthusiastic" about webcasting the execution, the source said. "That's why he's calling around, doing the Trump thing, asking people what they think." Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the plan on Real America's Voice. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it — that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said. Trump later publicly shifted his position, initially supporting the idea, then expressing nuance, and finally stating he would make the final decision.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that Trump has been receiving "negative input" from a bipartisan chorus of lawmakers and advisers, while The Free Press and Al Jazeera do not mention this input. The Daily Wire and The Dispatch do not mention Trump's private doubts, instead focusing on the moral and public implications of the execution. The Free Press and Al Jazeera both describe Hasan's attack as a mass shooting that killed 14 people, while Axios and The Daily Wire state 13 people were killed. The Free Press and Al Jazeera also note that Hasan was paralyzed from the waist down during the attack, a detail not included in Axios or The Daily Wire.

Sources Axios · The Daily Wire · The Dispatch · The Free Press · Al Jazeera · Washington Examiner

Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia

President Donald Trump announced a deal with Russia to supply diesel to the U.S. and global markets, including 300,000 tonnes immediately, 500,000 tonnes in November, and 1 million tonnes afterward. The agreement comes amid rising fuel prices and ahead of the midterm elections. Some lawmakers, including seven senators, criticized the deal as violating U.S. laws that prohibit Russian energy imports. Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in the future. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift to Putin" that funds Russia's war against Ukraine. The U.S. Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets remain frozen.

Republican Thomas Massie supported the deal, despite his adversarial relationship with Trump, while others like Thom Tillis argued the agreement undermines efforts to impose sanctions on Russia. The deal has also drawn criticism from a former NATO commander, who warned it could provide Putin with funds to continue the war in Ukraine. Analysts question whether Russia can deliver the promised quantities of diesel and whether it will significantly lower prices for American consumers.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that the U.S. uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day and that even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tonnes, it would only cover half of daily consumption. The Hill and FOX News both mention the 300,000 tonnes immediate release but differ in the context of the deal's timing, with FOX News noting the deal preceded Trump's "energy ceasefire" announcement. NPR states that Senator Jeanne Shaheen doubts the deal's authenticity and questions whether Russia has enough diesel to supply the U.S. ABC News does not mention the 300,000 tonnes figure or the 500,000 tonnes in November, focusing instead on the broader context of the deal and its political implications.

Sources BBC · The Hill · Washington Examiner · FOX News · NPR · ABC News

Trump and Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle after reports of improper conduct

U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle is under consideration for removal by President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio following multiple reports of alleged misconduct. A senior U.S. official stated that Trump and Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and are likely to decide on action this week. The official noted that Rubio, who visited Athens recently, was particularly upset, especially after Guilfoyle attended most of his events and greeted him with a bear hug as the allegations grew. The Wall Street Journal has previously reported on questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including alleged threats to a host country official, accepting improper gifts, and offering to use her influence in exchange for payment of a large credit card bill. Guilfoyle has not directly addressed the reports, though her lawyer has denied wrongdoing and the U.S. embassy in Athens has tacitly supported her.

Rubio initially defended Guilfoyle but later declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. After another report appeared, Rubio criticized journalists for asking about the allegations, stating he would not respond if he could not confirm their truth. The State Department’s inspector general is reportedly looking into the allegations, though it is unclear if a formal investigation has begun. Several Democratic lawmakers have called for an investigation into Guilfoyle’s conduct.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and BBC both report that Rubio was upset about Guilfoyle’s conduct and that the State Department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations. The Guardian adds that Rubio was particularly angry due to his recent visit to Athens and that Guilfoyle attended most of his events. The Washington Examiner mentions that Sen. John Barrasso predicted an inquiry into Guilfoyle’s conduct. The Mother Jones article includes quotes from Greek officials and details about Guilfoyle’s alleged use of “honey” in casual conversation, which are not present in other accounts. The FOX News account includes a quote from the Wall Street Journal about Guilfoyle suggesting the U.S. could undermine the Greek government, which is also mentioned in the Guardian and BBC. The ABC News account includes details about Deters’ legal history and his claim that he never made the payment, which are not included in the Guardian or BBC versions.

Sources The Guardian · Mother Jones · Washington Examiner · FOX News · ABC News · BBC

Texas Senate candidate James Talarico discusses flu absence in interviews as GOP sharpens attacks

James Talarico, a Texas Democratic Senate candidate, addressed his recent absence from the campaign trail in exclusive interviews on Sunday. He was spotted at the Austin City Limits Music Festival on Friday and attended a Kacey Musgrove concert in Dallas on Saturday. Talarico explained his absence as due to a severe case of the flu, which he said kept him away from public appearances for nearly two weeks. His campaign confirmed he had visited urgent care on Sept. 29 and saw his primary care physician the following week, though they did not specify the exact duration of his illness.

Talarico’s absence sparked online speculation, including claims that he had been secretly flown to Ohio for mental health treatment. These claims were debunked by the Lindner Center of Hope, which stated Talarico had never received treatment there. Talarico himself denied ever being in Ohio, re-sharing the center’s denial on social media. His campaign also clarified that he had been in New York for campaign events on Sept. 28 and was scheduled to appear at a fundraiser in Greenwich Village on that night, though it is unclear if he attended.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and New York Post both report that Talarico was seen at the Austin City Limits Music Festival on Oct. 9, while The Daily Wire and Axios do not mention this event. The Daily Wire claims Talarico was at a fundraiser in New York on Sept. 28 with Robert De Niro, a detail not included in the Washington Examiner or New York Post accounts. The Mother Jones article states that Talarico appeared remotely at an event on Sept. 30, citing his illness, while the New York Post and Washington Examiner note that he was seen in public on Sept. 30. The Daily Wire also mentions that Talarico’s campaign volunteers expressed concern about his absence, a detail not included in the other accounts.

Sources Washington Examiner · Mother Jones · New York Post · The Daily Wire · Axios · Newsweek

FBI Takes Action After Actress Accused Of Attacking Flight Attendants

Selma Blair, a 54-year-old actress known for roles in "Cruel Intentions," "Legally Blonde," and "Hellboy," was arrested after an alleged altercation on a Delta Air Lines flight from Los Angeles to New York. The FBI has issued a summons to Blair, accusing her of assault under federal law regarding incidents aboard the aircraft. She was taken into custody at JFK Airport following the flight, and her representative stated she experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct. The incident occurred around 11 p.m. on Delta Flight 938, with the pilot reporting "bite marks" and a "bloody nose" on the plane. Blair was transported to a hospital for evaluation and later arraigned on two counts of second-degree assault for allegedly kicking a police officer and a nurse after landing.

Blair has a history of incidents on flights, including a 2016 episode where she was removed from a Delta flight after an outburst, during which she reportedly mixed alcohol with medication and blacked out. She later apologized, acknowledging the mistake and expressing regret. In 2018, she was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis and has since become an advocate for disability rights.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and CBS News both mention Blair's 2016 incident and her apology, but only CBS News states that she was taken to a hospital and that she was transported on a stretcher. The Guardian and BBC report that Blair was taken to a hospital and that she was allegedly restrained on the plane by the flight crew. The New York Post adds that Blair missed multiple doses of a powerful medication and hit her head, leading to a state of "severe confusion and disorientation," a claim not made by other outlets. The Guardian also includes details about the alleged assault on a police officer and nurse, which are not explicitly mentioned in the Daily Wire or CBS News.

Sources The Daily Wire · NPR · BBC · CBS News · The Guardian · New York Post

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

RJ Mitte, actor best known for Breaking Bad, dies aged 34

RJ Mitte, the actor best known for his role as Walter White Jr. on the TV series *Breaking Bad*, has died at the age of 34. His representatives confirmed the news, stating that he took his own life. The actor, who lived with cerebral palsy, was praised for bringing authenticity to his role and for his advocacy for disability rights. Mitte appeared in 56 episodes of *Breaking Bad*, playing the son of Bryan Cranston’s character, Walter White. His co-stars, including Cranston, expressed deep grief over his death, with Cranston calling him “my sweet son on Breaking Bad” and noting their planned lunch meeting shortly before his death. Mitte also had roles in other series such as *Switched at Birth* and *The Guardians of Justice*, and was promoting his new film *Talking to Strangers* at the time of his death.

The Brownsville police department stated no foul play was suspected, and an autopsy was pending. Mitte was born in 1992 and was raised in Mississippi by adoptive parents. He spoke about his adoption in a 2016 interview with *The Guardian*, describing how he found out at age eight. He was also an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and president of the Mitte Foundation, which focused on disability advocacy.

Where the accounts differ

*The Guardian* and *ABC News* both state that Mitte died by suicide, while *The Daily Wire* and *CBS News* also mention suicide, though *The Daily Wire* notes an ongoing investigation. *The Guardian* and *CBS News* mention that Mitte was confirmed to have died by suicide by his representative, while *The Daily Wire* reports that the death was confirmed by TMZ and a county official. *The Guardian* and *ABC News* both state that Mitte was born in 1992 and raised in Mississippi, while *BBC* says he grew up in Louisiana. *The Daily Wire* and *CBS News* mention that Mitte was engaged to Kennedy Suarez and proposed in October 2025, a detail not included in *The Guardian* or *ABC News*. *The Guardian* and *BBC* note that Mitte’s character was based on a real person, a friend of Vince Gilligan, while *The Daily Wire* provides more detail about the character’s basis in a real person with more severe cerebral palsy.

Sources The Guardian · CBS News · BBC · Newsweek · ABC News · The Daily Wire

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

One dead and several injured after roller coaster incident at Six Flags Over Georgia

A man died on Monday after apparently falling out of a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, according to news reports. At least four other people were injured. Officials evacuated riders from the roller coaster at the amusement park, video footage posted on social media shows. A witness told a local news outlet that the man's body hit others on the ride before falling onto the roof of a haunted house attraction. A spokesperson for Six Flags Over Georgia said the park was "deeply saddened by the guest incident" and was cooperating with local authorities as they investigate what happened.

Cobb County Police confirmed Monday that a man died following an incident on the Goliath roller coaster at the Georgia amusement park, while several other injuries were also reported. Authorities have not released details about the cause of the incident. The incident happened around 4 p.m., and riders were evacuated from the coaster.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and Just The News do not mention the souvenir photo capturing the incident, while Newsweek, The Daily Wire, and FOX News describe the man appearing in a souvenir photo. The Daily Wire and The Guardian mention that the man was on the ride with a child, while the Washington Examiner and Just The News do not specify who was with the man. The Guardian and FOX News report the incident happened around 4 p.m., while the Washington Examiner and Just The News do not specify a time. The Guardian and The Daily Wire mention that the man fell and hit the car three different times, while the Washington Examiner and Just The News do not include this detail. The Guardian and The Daily Wire also mention that the man was on the ride with a child, while the Washington Examiner and Just The News do not specify who was with the man.

Sources Washington Examiner · Newsweek · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · Just The News · FOX News

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Hundreds of supermarkets in France hit by ‘unprecedented’ cyberattack disrupts food access for thousands.

Hundreds of French supermarkets hit by cyberattack causing fridge temperatures to rise to 50°C

A cyberattack on refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets caused fridges and freezers to heat up to as high as 50°C (122F), spoiling food and causing fires at several stores. The attack targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss, which allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely. Affected retailers include Intermarché, Cooperative U, Carrefour, Monoprix, and E Leclerc. The Paris prosecutor’s office described the incident as a “large-scale” cyberattack affecting “connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France.” The attack led to food losses and prompted Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to order an investigation by France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI). The attack also prompted calls for greater cybersecurity measures in the food supply chain.

The attack disrupted refrigeration systems, leading to the destruction of stocks of fresh and frozen products. Intermarché CEO Thierry Cotillard estimated the losses at “tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day.” Some stores had to throw away all affected products, while others were working to restore normal operations. The attack also caused issues for staff arriving at stores, with some encountering hot air from freezers and even small fires. The full scale of the attack remains unclear, but estimates suggest around 400 stores were affected out of 15,000 in France.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera reports that Intermarché said at least 300 shops of its Netto brand were targeted, along with more than 100 Cooperative U outlets, while BBC states that Intermarché and its Netto brand affected 180 stores, with another 100 urgently disconnected from the internet. Al Jazeera also mentions that Carrefour said 80 supermarkets were affected, while BBC reports Carrefour said fridges in 80 of its 6,000 stores were hacked. Al Jazeera notes that Monoprix said about 5 percent of its roughly 490 stores were hit, while BBC states Monoprix said 5% of its 400-plus stores were affected. Al Jazeera reports that E Leclerc said several of its stores were targeted, while BBC does not specify the number of E Leclerc stores affected. BBC mentions that Danfoss did not confirm how warm the fridges and freezers could become, while Al Jazeera states that the fridges warmed to 50°C. BBC also reports that two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of €270,000, which Al Jazeera does not mention.

Sources Al Jazeera · BBC

Mullin spurns martyrdom concerns from livestreamed execution: ‘No one has to watch’

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin rejected the idea that livestreaming the execution of the Fort Hood mass shooter Nidal Malik Hasan could make him a martyr for his cause, saying those against the idea do not have to watch. Mullin told CBS News’s Face the Nation on Sunday that he sees no “elevated risk” of radicalization in the United States brought on by livestreaming the firing squad execution in December.

FOX News reported that the U.S. government intends to take Nidal Hasan to a firing range at Fort Hood and publicly execute him by firing squad in December. The outlet also noted that Americans will be able to watch the execution on live stream, which has transformed the conclusion of one of the darkest chapters in the Army's history into a more uncomfortable question about how a nation should reckon with the gravity of taking a life, even when that life belongs to a mass murderer.

Axios highlighted that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's announcement to livestream the execution reflects a shift toward putting raw, real-world violence on display for unlimited audiences. The outlet noted that this would be the first known public broadcast of a lawful execution, according to death penalty experts, and that tech companies like TikTok and Kick have said livestreaming the event would violate their policies.

Where the accounts differ

Washington Examiner omits any mention of the planned livestream and focuses solely on Mullin’s comments about the execution not making Hasan a martyr. FOX News includes details about the planned livestream and quotes Fort Hood victim Alonzo Lunsford, who survived being shot seven times by Hasan, about his views on the execution. Axios provides context about the broader trend of making violent events public and the potential implications for tech companies and free speech.

Sources Washington Examiner · FOX News · Axios · New York Post · The Guardian · NPR

Trump calls for Ukraine to replace Zelensky after criticizing diesel deal with Russia

President Donald Trump said on Saturday that it is "time for Ukraine to get a new president" after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky criticized a U.S.-Russia diesel deal. Trump accused Zelensky of failing to reach a peace agreement with Russia and of continuing to authorize attacks on Russian refineries. The deal, announced earlier in the week, allows Russia to resume diesel exports to the U.S. and global markets, with an initial 300,000 tonnes to be released by early April. Zelensky warned that the deal would provide Moscow with additional funds to continue its war in Ukraine.

Zelensky accused Russia of using the deal to justify continued attacks on Ukrainian cities, including a deadly strike on Zaporizhzhia that killed at least 20 people. He argued that the deal would allow Russia to fund its military operations, including the production of weapons and recruitment of mercenaries. The U.S. administration confirmed the agreement, with Trump stating it was part of an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that Trump suggested Ukraine should "get a new leader who can make a deal" and that Zelensky accused Russia of using the deal to continue its war. Straight Arrow News adds that Zelensky directly linked the attack in Zaporizhzhia to the diesel deal, stating Russia "said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia." The Hill and New York Post include details about the attack, including the number of casualties and the timing relative to the diesel deal announcement. Washington Examiner and Axios note Republican backlash against the deal, with Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick introducing legislation to block Russian oil purchases. The Hill also mentions Rep. Michael McCaul’s criticism of the deal, while Axios attributes the same concern to McCaul and adds that Fitzpatrick is using a discharge petition to force a vote.

Sources BBC · Straight Arrow News · Washington Examiner · Axios · The Hill · New York Post

Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport kills 12, injures over 300

A missile strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. The attack, which occurred on Saturday, targeted a complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights. The victims included four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, and one person each from the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan, and Egypt. The Saudi government suspended airport operations and warned citizens to avoid the facility. The attack is part of a series of strikes on Saudi infrastructure, with the Houthis claiming responsibility for several recent attacks. The United States condemned the attack, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling it a “reprehensible attack” and expressing support for Saudi Arabia. President Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the Houthis.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and CBS News both report that the attack killed 12 people, including one American, and injured 300. The Guardian and NPR report the same numbers but note that the attack was the deadliest in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war. The Washington Examiner and New York Post both mention the American victim but do not specify the exact number of casualties. The Guardian and NPR report that the attack was the deadliest in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war, while Al Jazeera and CBS News do not make this claim. The New York Post and Washington Examiner attribute the attack to the Houthis, while the Guardian and NPR do not explicitly name the attackers, though they imply the Houthis were responsible.

Sources Al Jazeera · New York Post · CBS News · Washington Examiner · The Guardian · NPR

Four dead and thousands without power after Hurricane Isaias lashes US

Hurricane Isaias made landfall in Florida on Friday as a Category 2 storm with maximum sustained winds of 105mph (168km/h), causing widespread damage, power outages, and at least four deaths. The storm weakened to a post-tropical cyclone by Saturday, with officials reporting two deaths each in Alabama and Florida. In Florida, a woman died when a tree fell on her home, and another person died from carbon monoxide poisoning after running a generator in a garage. In Alabama, two deaths were reported, though details were not provided. The storm caused extensive damage, including roof destruction, flooded roads, and downed trees. Power outages affected hundreds of thousands of people across Florida, Alabama, and Georgia, with some areas experiencing over 900,000 outages. Officials warned of ongoing flood risks and potential tornadoes as the storm moved inland.

Where the accounts differ

BBC and The Guardian both report four deaths, with two in Florida and two in Alabama. The Daily Wire and NPR report at least two deaths, with the Daily Wire specifying one in Florida and one in Alabama, while NPR confirms four deaths but does not specify the states. The Guardian and BBC provide more details on the causes of death, including carbon monoxide poisoning and tree-related incidents. The Daily Caller focuses on the impact of the storm on fuel supply and does not mention the number of deaths. The Guardian and BBC mention specific locations for deaths, while NPR and The Daily Wire do not. The Guardian and BBC attribute the deaths in Alabama to trees falling on homes, while NPR and The Daily Wire do not specify the cause of the Alabama deaths beyond a tree falling on a house.

Sources BBC · The Daily Wire · The Daily Caller · The Guardian · NPR · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Pope Leo XIV to undergo lung surgery this week

Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday that he will have surgery this week to remove a "localized nodule" in his lung. The procedure is expected to take place at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, where popes typically receive medical attention. The Vatican spokesperson, Matteo Bruni, stated the surgery is scheduled for the first days of the week, with a recovery time of about one week. The Pope also mentioned his upcoming international trip to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru in November, though it is unclear if the surgery will affect his itinerary.

The Pope described the nodule as found at a "very early stage" and emphasized that doctors recommended the surgery. He thanked the faithful for their spiritual support and entrusted himself to their prayers. The American Cancer Society defines a lung nodule as a small abnormal area, less than or equal to 3 cm, found during a CT scan. Dr. Panagis Galiatsatos, a pulmonary physician, noted that most lung nodules are benign and that surgery is considered when there is significant concern for cancer.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and CBS News both report that the Pope described the nodule as "localized" and found at an "early stage," but CBS News adds that the nodule was "circumscribed," a term not used by NPR. FOX News refers to the nodule as a "tumor," a term not used by the other outlets. The Daily Caller mentions the nodule was "contained within a single area of the lung," a detail not included in the other accounts. Straight Arrow News includes a reference to the Pope's statement on the death penalty, which is not mentioned in the other accounts. BBC notes that the Pope's predecessor, Pope Francis, had a history of lung issues, a detail not included in the other accounts.

Sources NPR · CBS News · BBC · Straight Arrow News · FOX News · The Daily Caller

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Judge orders the Trump administration to cancel taxpayer-funded promotional TV ads

A federal judge in New York ordered the Trump administration to cancel any remaining taxpayer-funded television commercials promoting his political message. The order, issued by U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon, came after a coalition including Common Cause and Democracy Forward challenged the ads as an illegal misuse of funds. The judge granted a temporary restraining order, instructing the administration to stop any further development, creation, or airing of the ads for two weeks. The Department of Homeland Security allocated $20 million in taxpayer money for the campaign, which began in late September and includes ads glorifying Trump and echoing his political messaging.

The White House defended the ads as public service announcements, similar to past efforts by previous administrations. However, critics argue the recent ads differ from typical public service announcements because they do not aim to help the public benefit from specific government programs. The use of public funds for the ads drew criticism from some Republicans, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who stated, "It shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars." The Democratic National Committee has also sued the administration over the ads.

Where the accounts differ

ABC News and CBS News both report that the judge ordered the administration to cancel the ads and that the Department of Homeland Security allocated $20 million for the campaign. CBS News adds that the funds were allocated for a "National Media Campaign" starting on Sept. 20 and that the White House Office of Management and Budget granted DHS's Customs and Border Protection $20 million for "OBBB Commemorative Events," according to a nongovernment database. ABC News does not mention these specific allocations. Axios reports that the ruling stems from a suit filed by Common Cause, Democracy Forward, and others in the Southern District of New York, and that a similar lawsuit was filed by the Democratic National Committee in D.C. federal court. CBS News and ABC News do not mention the Democratic National Committee's lawsuit.

Sources ABC News · CBS News · Axios

No source labeled lean-right or left or right covered this story.

U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle Faces Allegations of Misconduct and Ethics Violations

Kimberly Guilfoyle, U.S. Ambassador to Greece, is under scrutiny following multiple reports alleging improper conduct. The Wall Street Journal has published three reports detailing claims that she sought a $100,000 credit card payment from a Trump donor in exchange for political favors. These allegations include offering access to administration officials and assistance with legal and tax issues. The State Department’s Office of Inspector General is reportedly investigating whether she accepted gifts or favors from private businessmen.

The allegations have drawn attention from both Republican and Democratic officials. Senator Marco Rubio, the Secretary of State, has expressed frustration over the reports, particularly after visiting Athens and attending events with Guilfoyle. Democratic lawmakers, including Rep. Gregory Meeks and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, have called for investigations into her conduct. The White House is reportedly considering her removal, with some officials describing their anger over the allegations.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and FOX News both report that Sen. John Barrasso suggested an investigation into Guilfoyle, while The Guardian and Mother Jones do not mention Barrasso’s comments. The Daily Caller includes specific details about Guilfoyle’s attendance at the World Economic Forum and her interactions with Greek tycoons, which are not mentioned in the Washington Examiner or FOX News accounts. The Guardian and Mother Jones provide more context about the nature of the alleged threats to Greek officials, while The Daily Caller and FOX News focus on her luxury travel and interactions with wealthy businessmen. The Guardian and Mother Jones attribute the claim about Guilfoyle asking a Trump donor to wire $100,000 to the Wall Street Journal, while The Daily Caller and FOX News also cite the Journal but add details about her interactions with the donor.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Daily Caller · The Guardian · FOX News · Mother Jones

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Donald Trump Says He Would 'Love' to Have John Fetterman as a Republican

President Donald Trump said Saturday he would "love" to see Democratic Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania become a Republican, renewing speculation about the senator's future. Trump described Fetterman as a "very solid person" with "great common sense" and "magnificent parents." The comments were among Trump's clearest public efforts yet to encourage Fetterman to join the GOP at a time when control of the Senate remains in play ahead of next month's midterm elections. Fetterman has consistently said he does not intend to become a Republican, though he has frequently frustrated fellow Democrats by breaking with the party on several issues, including immigration and support for Israel.

Fetterman has repeatedly rejected the notion of becoming a Republican, writing in The Washington Post in May that he would be a "terrible Republican who still votes overwhelmingly with Democrats." Despite this, he has made appearances at Republican events and recorded a video for a Republican midterm convention praising fellow Pennsylvania Sen. Dave McCormick. Polling shows Fetterman has stronger support among Republican voters than among Democrats, with 73% of Pennsylvania Republicans viewing him favorably compared to 22% of Democrats.

Where the accounts differ

Newsweek and The Guardian both report that Trump said Fetterman "does better as a Republican than he does as a Democrat." FOX News and the Washington Examiner also include this line, though FOX News adds that Trump said "it’s going to be hard for him to get the nomination as a Democrat." The New York Post and Washington Examiner mention that Trump described Fetterman as a "great guy" with "magnificent parents," while The Guardian and Newsweek include this characterization as well. The Washington Examiner and FOX News report that Fetterman has voted with Democrats 81% of the time during the current session, while Newsweek and The Guardian state he has voted with Democrats 90% of the time since joining the Senate in 2023.

Sources Newsweek · FOX News · New York Post · Washington Examiner · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-left covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: At least 139 people dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, U.N. Says (massive loss of life impacting families and highlighting unsafe migration conditions)

Children among 139 dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, UN says

A boat carrying 305 migrants from Djibouti to Yemen capsized near Obock on Thursday night, resulting in at least 139 deaths and dozens missing, according to the UN's migration office. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) reported that around 82 people were rescued. All survivors, identified as Ethiopian nationals, received medical care and psychological support. The IOM revised its death toll from 109 to 139 after recovering 30 more bodies. The incident highlights the dangers faced by migrants seeking work in Gulf countries, with tens of thousands making the journey annually.

The IOM noted that the boat sank due to overcrowding, with the incident occurring shortly after departure on the evening of October 8. Survivors were taken to an IOM rescue center in Obock. The IOM's Djibouti mission chief, Alexandre Coissac, described the tragedy as a "stark reminder" of the risks migrants face. The IOM also mentioned that the crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula is a common but dangerous route, with more than 900 migrants dying or going missing along the route last year.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that the boat capsized near Obock on Thursday night, while FOX News states the capsizing occurred "Thursday night or early Friday" near Guhere, north of Obock. BBC mentions that the IOM revised its toll from 109 to 139 after recovering 30 more bodies, whereas FOX News notes that the confirmed death toll includes only victims buried by authorities and may rise as additional bodies are verified. FOX News also includes a quote from IOM Chief of Mission Alexandre Coissac stating that some victims were buried without names in a common grave, a detail not mentioned in BBC.

Sources BBC · FOX News
