Student protests erupt at Cornell over mishandling of gang-rape allegations

Protests erupted at Cornell University on Monday as students criticized officials for their handling of gang-rape allegations, demanding the president’s resignation and painting “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” on an administrative building. The demonstrations were sparked by a high-profile case involving a former student, known as Jane Doe, who alleged she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in 2024. Protesters called for the banning of fraternities and criticized the university for failing to protect students. The vandalism at Day Hall, the building housing the president’s office, included messages like “AT CORNELL RAPISTS ARE PROTECTED PROTESTORS ARE EXPELLED.” The university condemned the vandalism, stating it was not the answer to expressing concerns.

The case has drawn international attention, with critics accusing Cornell of being too lenient with the accused men and failing the victim. According to lawyers for Jane Doe, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the incident, while others faced suspensions or required to write reflection papers. The university has faced backlash for its handling of the case, with students and faculty demanding stronger action against sexual violence on campus.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that four student demonstrators were suspended in 2024, while CBS News and The New York Post do not mention any suspensions. The Guardian attributes the painted messages to students protesting the treatment of pro-Palestine protesters, while FOX News and The Daily Wire do not mention this context. The Daily Wire claims Jane Doe consented to the sexual activity and later retroactively claimed she was assaulted, a claim not mentioned in other accounts. The New York Post and The Guardian describe the alleged incident as a gang rape, while CBS News and The Daily Wire do not specify the nature of the alleged assault beyond the presence of ketamine.

Sources The Guardian · CBS News · FOX News · The Daily Wire · Straight Arrow News · New York Post

US death row inmate Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyers say

Christa Pike, a 50-year-old death row inmate in Tennessee, survived a failed execution attempt last week, according to her lawyers. She was administered two doses of pentobarbital, a barbiturate used in lethal injections, but did not die. Pike, who was convicted in 1996 for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, remains in critical condition in a Nashville hospital, intubated and on a ventilator. Her lawyers reported that she is "conscious and speaking" and has suffered "severe damage" to her arms. The Tennessee Department of Correction has halted all executions in the state and ordered an independent investigation following the botched attempt.

Pike’s legal team had previously warned that her medical history, including a blood-clotting condition and small veins, made lethal injection a risky and potentially painful method. They had sought alternative execution methods, such as hanging or a firing squad, but the Supreme Court overruled a stay of execution. The failed attempt has raised questions about the reliability and humanity of lethal injection as a method of execution.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that Pike is "conscious and speaking" and that experts and her legal team say her recovery is "unprecedented." Mother Jones states that Pike "remains intubated, on a ventilator" and that her arms are "swollen, burned and blistered." The Nation says Pike "has not spoken since the failed execution." These accounts differ on Pike’s current state of consciousness and physical condition.

Sources BBC · Mother Jones · The Daily Wire · The Dispatch · Slate · The Nation

Supreme Court Begins New Term With Major Cases On Immigration, Gun Rights, Climate Lawsuits

The Supreme Court opened its new term Monday with a series of high-profile cases that include challenges to President Trump’s immigration policies, gun control measures, and climate-related lawsuits. The justices are also facing political pressure as Trump criticizes his appointees and Democrats consider changes to the Court. The term includes cases on Arizona’s voter registration requirements, the legality of deporting migrants to third countries, and the constitutionality of AR-15 bans. The Court also began its term with a major climate case, Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, where Boulder, Colorado, seeks to hold energy companies liable for climate damages.

The Court’s emergency docket has become increasingly important as the justices consider urgent issues related to elections and immigration. The administration’s immigration policies face two major tests, with the Court set to hear cases on mandatory detention for certain immigrants and the legality of deporting migrants to countries where they are not citizens. The Court has allowed deportations to continue while the litigation proceeds. The term also includes a case on the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style weapons and a climate case that could affect dozens of similar lawsuits nationwide.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and Axios both mention the Court’s consideration of Arizona’s voter registration requirements and the administration’s immigration policies, but only Axios explicitly states that the Court allowed the administration to restart third-country deportations. The Daily Wire does not mention this specific action. The Daily Caller and Slate provide more detailed accounts of the climate case, including the arguments and the involvement of specific justices, while FOX News and The Daily Wire focus more on the broader implications and legal arguments without the same level of detail on the case specifics.

Sources The Daily Wire · Axios · FOX News · The Daily Caller · Slate · NPR

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Three Years After October 7, Survivors and Analysts Reflect on the Attacks and Their Aftermath

The third anniversary of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel has prompted renewed reflection on the event and its consequences. Survivors like Keith Siegel, who was held hostage for 484 days, describe the trauma of the attacks and the ongoing struggle to rebuild. The attacks resulted in the deaths of 1,209 people, including 36 children, and the abduction of 251 individuals, with 47 killed and 76 taken to Gaza in the kibbutz of Nir Oz. The event has also sparked debates about Israel’s military response and the broader regional implications. Analysts, including those from The Washington Examiner, have discussed the long-term strategic impact on Israel and the Middle East, noting the country’s military successes against Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran. Meanwhile, other outlets have focused on the human toll, the political fallout, and the international context of the conflict.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner reports on the decline in nontraditional sexual identity among young Americans, citing a drop in "LGB" identification among high schoolers and a decline in bisexual, transgender, and queer identifications among students aged 14-25. The Guardian focuses on the personal trauma of survivors, including Keith Siegel’s experience as a hostage and the broader impact on the kibbutz of Nir Oz. The Free Press highlights the memoir of Avinatan Or, a Hamas hostage, detailing his captivity and survival. The Daily Wire provides an analysis of Hamas’s founding charter, emphasizing its religious motivations and framing the conflict as a religious struggle. NPR reports on new revelations that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was warned about the potential Hamas attack, while Al Jazeera focuses on the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, detailing the devastation and ongoing suffering of the population.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Guardian · The Free Press · The Daily Wire · NPR · Al Jazeera

Hasan Piker says 9/11 remark ‘far less damaging’ than Trump’s ‘take out’ LA and San Diego

Hasan Piker, a left-wing Twitch streamer and member of the Democratic Socialists of America, compared his 2019 remark that America "deserved" 9/11 to President Donald Trump’s comments suggesting Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego. Piker claimed his remark was not nearly as harmful as Trump’s. Trump made the remarks during a campaign rally in Nebraska, defending the war with Iran and suggesting the conflict was a "small price to pay" for safety. The comments drew swift condemnation from California officials, including Governor Gavin Newsom, who called them "deranged and dangerous." The White House later attempted to clarify that Trump was not suggesting Iran should attack U.S. cities, but rather that the U.S. was fighting to prevent Iran from doing so.

Where the accounts differ

The Washington Examiner and Newsweek both report that Piker claimed his 2019 remark was less damaging than Trump’s comments. The Washington Examiner adds that Piker speculated Democrats would not go after Trump for his remarks, while Newsweek notes that Piker apologized for the remark, clarifying it was about U.S. foreign policy, not the victims of 9/11. The Guardian and CBS News do not mention Piker’s comparison or apology. The ABC News and Newsweek accounts differ in that Newsweek states the White House defended Trump, while ABC News reports that the White House’s Rapid Response account denied Trump’s remarks were suggesting Iran should attack U.S. cities.

Sources Washington Examiner · The Guardian · ABC News · CBS News · Newsweek · BBC

U.S. officials monitor suspected plague case in Russia after researcher dies

A Russian lab technician died after contracting pneumonia, prompting U.S. officials to closely monitor the situation. The Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk is under scrutiny as the cause of death remains unclear. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated the administration is watching the situation but emphasized there is no cause for alarm. The U.S. government is assessing options and has its most serious travel warning in place for Russia due to the war with Ukraine. The incident has raised concerns about global biological threats and the need for pandemic preparedness. Russian authorities have placed nearly 200 people under medical observation and quarantined several hospitals following the death. The Russian health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said no microorganisms linked to the woman's work were found in her biological samples. The World Health Organization (WHO) was informed that no plague or other high-threat pathogen was detected among her close contacts, though confirmation is pending.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that the cause of death is "pneumonia of undetermined etiology" and that there are conflicting accounts of how the researcher got sick. It also mentions the possibility of a genetically altered strain of plague and the need for more information to determine the appropriate response. BBC states that the cause of death was "pneumonia of undetermined etiology" and that no microorganisms linked to her work were found in her biological samples. It also notes that the Russian health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, found no emergency situation at the institute. Straight Arrow News provides more specific details about the deceased, Daria Shipilova, and mentions that she broke a test tube containing the pathogen. New York Post and FOX News both mention the possibility of a bioweapon and antibiotic resistance, with FOX News citing a former senior Trump official warning that the case could be "far worse" than the plague. Washington Examiner focuses on Trump's planned call with Putin and the U.S. government's willingness to help Russia contain any possible outbreak.

Sources Axios · BBC · Straight Arrow News · New York Post · Washington Examiner · FOX News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Disgraced Former House Speaker Dead At 84

Dennis Hastert, the longest-serving Republican House Speaker, has died at 84, according to a local coroner. He died at his home over the weekend. Hastert, who served as House Speaker from 1999 to 2007, was known for his role in shaping President George W. Bush’s legislative agenda. He later admitted to sexually abusing boys during his time as a high school wrestling coach and was sentenced to prison for financial crimes related to hush money payments. He was released from federal prison in 2017.

Hastert was born in 1942 and worked as a teacher and wrestling coach at Yorkville High School before entering politics. He was elected to the Illinois House of Representatives and then to the U.S. House in 1986. He became House Speaker after Newt Gingrich stepped down in 1998 and Bob Livingston resigned due to extramarital affairs. He led the House until Republicans lost their majority in 2006. After resigning from Congress in 2007, he worked as a lobbyist until his indictment in 2015 for financial crimes.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and CBS News both state that Hastert was the highest-ranking elected U.S. official to serve a prison sentence, while FOX News and Straight Arrow News do not mention this claim. The Daily Wire and CBS News attribute the claim about the prison sentence to the U.S. attorney, Zachary Fardon, while FOX News and Straight Arrow News do not attribute the claim to any specific source. ABC News and Axios do not mention the claim about being the highest-ranking official to serve prison time.

Sources The Daily Wire · FOX News · ABC News · CBS News · Axios · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump says 'threat' led US to pull bombers from RAF Fairford

The US military removed its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, England, following a threat to the base, according to President Donald Trump. The Pentagon confirmed the bombers, thought to be about a dozen, were moved back to their home stations in the US. Trump stated the decision was made due to intelligence suggesting a threat, though he did not specify its nature. The move came after a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the airbase. The exact nature of the threat remains unclear, but sources in Washington speculated it might have involved sabotage or an attack on the bombers in the event of resumed hostilities with Iran.

The incident at RAF Fairford led to the arrest of five men and a sixth British-Iranian national, all released on bail. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested there were "strong indications" Iran was involved, while Iran denied any role. The US still maintains the ability to strike Iran with its remaining forces in the Middle East. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the movement of the bombers as a routine rotation, while Vice President JD Vance linked the decision to an "abundance of caution" against Iran.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that Trump refused to be drawn on the nature of the threat, while ABC News states Trump said "we know who made the threat" but did not confirm the identity. Straight Arrow News claims the withdrawal was connected to existing threat reporting, not a new threat, whereas The New York Post and The Daily Wire describe the move as a response to new intelligence about an Iran-backed plot. The Guardian does not specify the nature of the threat or the exact number of bombers moved, while The Daily Wire mentions that some aircraft left while aerial refueling was still in progress.

Sources BBC · ABC News · Straight Arrow News · New York Post · The Daily Wire · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: A former CIA official defrauded taxpayers of $200 million by faking classified programs, directly impacting millions through lost public funds.

Ex-US spy who stashed gold bars in his home admits to $200m scam

A former CIA officer, David Rush, 49, pleaded guilty to wire fraud after admitting to defrauding the US government of nearly $200 million. Prosecutors stated that Rush created fake classified programs to justify the acquisition of luxury real estate, gold bars, and other assets. During an FBI raid in May, agents found 298 gold bars, $2 million in cash, and 35 luxury watches at his home. Rush also confessed to providing top secret data to a foreign government official, which could have endangered a clandestine human source.

Rush admitted to fabricating a "Special Access Program" to justify expenditures, including the purchase of four Florida properties and luxury vehicles. Court filings indicate he used fraudulent public funds to acquire these assets and directed wire transfers totaling $145 million. Prosecutors said he used the funds to buy real estate, which he intended to resell for profit. The plea deal requires Rush to forfeit the gold bars, cash, real estate, vehicles, and watches, as well as pay restitution to the government.

Where the accounts differ

BBC and The Daily Wire both report that Rush admitted to providing top secret data to a foreign government official, while Just The News and FOX News attribute the disclosure of the clandestine human source to Rush. The Daily Wire and CBS News mention the $194 million figure, while BBC and FOX News cite $200 million. The Washington Examiner and CBS News do not specify the exact amount of the fraud, only that it was nearly $200 million. The Daily Wire and CBS News mention the $45 million wire transfer, while BBC and FOX News refer to it as part of the $200 million scheme. The Daily Wire and CBS News also note that Rush lied about his education and military background, while BBC and FOX News do not mention this detail.

Sources BBC · The Daily Wire · Washington Examiner · CBS News · FOX News · Just The News

No source labeled left covered this story.

The brief ends here.

Fort Hood shooter to be executed by firing squad - a first for US military since World War Two

The Pentagon has announced it will execute a former US Army major by firing squad, the first such military execution in more than 60 years. Nidal Malik Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on social media on Monday that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had made the recommendation and President Donald Trump approved it. The execution will mark the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two. Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, killed 13 soldiers at the base in Texas in 2009 and later admitted in court he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan. The attack on 5 November 2009 was the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base. The attack took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines. Hasan is currently one of four inmates on the US military's death row. A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law.

Where the accounts differ

BBC states the execution will be the first since the end of World War Two, while The Hill says it will be the first since 1961. The Guardian and Newsweek do not specify the exact year of the last military execution by firing squad. Just The News and FOX News both mention 1961 as the last military execution by firing squad. The Guardian and Newsweek differ in the number of casualties, with the Guardian stating 12 soldiers and 30 wounded, while Newsweek says 13 dead and more than 30 wounded. FOX News attributes the claim that Hasan said "I shot to kill" to a Sanity Board report, while the other accounts do not mention this. The Guardian and Newsweek provide more detail about Hasan's background and mental state, while FOX News includes information about Hasan's alleged visit to a strip club and his actions during the attack.

Sources BBC · Just The News · The Guardian · Newsweek · The Hill · FOX News

Christa Pike survived failed execution attempt in Tennessee

Christa Pike, a convicted murderer, was scheduled for lethal injection in Tennessee on September 30, 2026. The execution was halted by a federal court stay just before it began, leading to a nine-hour wait at the prison. After the stay was lifted, Pike was taken to the death chamber, where she was administered two doses of pentobarbital. She remained conscious for part of the process, breathing heavily and snoring, before being taken to a hospital. Her lawyer, Stephen Ferrell, stated she remains critically ill and unconscious, with an unclear prognosis. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year following the botched attempt.

Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate. Her lawyers had previously warned that her medical condition, including a platelet disorder and small veins, made lethal injection a risky and potentially painful method. The state had previously botched an execution attempt in May 2026 with Tony Carruthers, leading to a suspension of executions. The Department of Correction's communications director, Dorinda Carter, announced the execution was proceeding after the stay was lifted.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that the execution was halted by a federal court stay and that the process took place in the death chamber with witnesses present. BBC and The Nation describe Pike as remaining unconscious and critically ill, with her lawyer stating the prognosis is unclear. The Nation adds that Pike's lawyers had warned about the risks of lethal injection due to her medical history. Straight Arrow News mentions that prison officials followed a protocol requiring a second dose if the first failed, leading to life-saving measures. Washington Examiner and New York Post note that Pike may not fully recover and that her condition remains critical. The Nation also highlights the broader context of botched executions in Tennessee and the state's history of failed attempts.

Sources NPR · BBC · Washington Examiner · New York Post · The Nation · Straight Arrow News

Jim Bakker, famed televangelist felled by scandal, dies at age 86

Jim Bakker, the televangelist who built a Christian broadcasting empire before it collapsed in scandal, has died at the age of 86. His second wife, Lori Bakker, announced his death on social media, stating he "went home to be with the Lord." Bakker and his first wife, Tammy Faye Bakker, became one of television's most recognized couples with their PTL show, which preached to millions of viewers that Christian faith and financial success were compatible. Their success led to the launch of an amusement park-like community in North Carolina. Bakker's world came crashing down in 1987 when he admitted to a sexual relationship with a secretary named Jessica Hahn, who accused him of abuse. A year later, he was indicted on federal financial charges and spent five years in prison. Bakker returned to television ministry and married Lori.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that Bakker was sentenced to 45 years in prison but the sentence was later reduced, while Newsweek states he was sentenced to 45 years and later received a reduced sentence of eight years. The Guardian and ABC News mention that Bakker was convicted of defrauding followers of $158 million, while Newsweek states the amount was $158 million. The Guardian and The Guardian also note that Bakker was defrocked after the sexual encounter with Jessica Hahn, while Newsweek attributes this to Bakker's own statement that he was "set up" by former colleagues. The Guardian and The Guardian also mention that Bakker was defrocked after the sexual encounter with Jessica Hahn, while Newsweek attributes this to Bakker's own statement that he was "set up" by former colleagues.

Sources Just The News · The Guardian · NPR · ABC News · CBS News · Newsweek

Obama to campaign with fellow Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in key Michigan Senate race

Former President Barack Obama will campaign alongside Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit on October 24, according to multiple outlets. The event will also feature Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who is running for governor. The Senate race is considered one of the most competitive in the midterm cycle, with the outcome potentially determining control of the Senate. Obama has been selective in his campaign appearances since leaving office but has increased his public presence in the final stretch of high-stakes elections.

Obama’s involvement in the race follows a pattern of increased participation in recent midterms, including appearances in Detroit during the 2022 and 2024 elections. He has also recorded a series of campaign ads for Democratic candidates, which will be released in the coming weeks. The event is expected to draw large crowds and prominent guests, with some outlets noting that Obama’s presence could provide a significant boost to El-Sayed’s campaign, particularly in Detroit, where he remains highly popular.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and The Daily Wire report that El-Sayed’s campaign has faced scrutiny over past statements, including a resurfaced video clip where he criticized Mackinac Island. The Daily Wire attributes this to El-Sayed, while The Guardian does not mention the clip. The Guardian also notes that El-Sayed has made opposition to US military aid to Israel and criticism of its conduct in Gaza central to his campaign, a detail absent in other accounts. The Nation highlights that El-Sayed’s opponent, Mike Rogers, falsely claimed he had pledged support to the Muslim Brotherhood and said “America deserved 9/11,” which The Daily Wire attributes to Rogers, while The Guardian does not mention these claims.

Sources Just The News · ABC News · New York Post · The Daily Wire · The Guardian · The Nation

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor launches legal action against police over Epstein raids
